tips.title: Volumes must be in dm³
tips.body: Concentration is *per **dm³***, so a volume in cm³ has to be divided by **1000** first. $25\text{ cm}^3$ is $0.025\text{ dm}^3$. Forgetting this is the single commonest error in titration calculations, and it puts the answer out by a factor of a thousand.

tips.title: Moles = concentration × volume
tips.body: $$n = c \times V$$ with $c$ in mol/dm³ and $V$ in dm³. Rearranged, $c = n \div V$ and $V = n \div c$. Every titration calculation is this equation used twice — once forwards on the solution you know, once backwards on the one you do not.

tips.title: Two units of concentration
tips.body: **g/dm³** is mass per volume; **mol/dm³** is amount per volume. Convert between them with the $M_r$: *g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × $M_r$*, and divide to go back. A question that gives grams and asks for mol/dm³ needs both steps.

tips.title: Concordant titres only
tips.body: Average only the titres that agree within **0.10 cm³** of each other. A rough first titration and any outlier are **excluded**, and you should say that you excluded them. Averaging everything drags the mean towards the rough run and loses marks.

tips.title: The equation gives the ratio
tips.body: Acid moles equal alkali moles **only when the ratio is 1 : 1**. For $\mathrm{H_2SO_4} + 2\mathrm{NaOH}$ there are **twice** as many moles of alkali as acid. Check the balanced equation before assuming the amounts match.

steps.title: Concentration in g/dm³
steps.body:
A solution's **concentration** says how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution.

The simplest measure is **mass per unit volume**, in **grams per dm³**:

$$\text{concentration (g/dm}^3) = \frac{\text{mass of solute (g)}}{\text{volume of solution (dm}^3)}$$

**A dm³ is 1000 cm³** — the same as a litre. Laboratory volumes are measured in cm³, so almost every question needs a conversion first: divide the cm³ by 1000.

$25\text{ g}$ of solute in $500\text{ cm}^3$:

- volume $= 500 \div 1000 = 0.5\text{ dm}^3$
- concentration $= \dfrac{25}{0.5} = 50\text{ g/dm}^3$

**More solute in the same volume, or the same solute in less solution, means a higher concentration.** Concentration does not depend on how much of the solution you take: a spoonful and a bucketful of the same solution have the same concentration.

**Rearranged**, $\text{mass} = \text{concentration} \times \text{volume}$, which is how you find the mass of solute in a given volume.

steps.title: Concentration in mol/dm³
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)*

Chemists usually want the **amount** of solute rather than its mass, because reactions happen in mole ratios. Concentration in **mol/dm³** gives exactly that:

$$\text{concentration (mol/dm}^3) = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution (dm}^3)}$$

which rearranges to the form used most often:

$$n = c \times V$$

**Converting between the two units** uses the relative formula mass:

- $\text{g/dm}^3 = \text{mol/dm}^3 \times M_r$
- $\text{mol/dm}^3 = \text{g/dm}^3 \div M_r$

A solution of sodium hydroxide at $0.08\text{ mol/dm}^3$ ($M_r = 40$) is $0.08 \times 40 = 3.2\text{ g/dm}^3$.

**Watch the units in the question.** "Concentration" alone is ambiguous; the unit tells you which calculation is wanted. A question giving a **mass** and asking for **mol/dm³** needs two steps: mass to moles, then moles per dm³.

**Worked example.** $4\text{ g}$ of sodium hydroxide dissolved to make $250\text{ cm}^3$:

- moles $= \dfrac{4}{40} = 0.1\text{ mol}$
- volume $= 0.25\text{ dm}^3$
- concentration $= \dfrac{0.1}{0.25} = 0.4\text{ mol/dm}^3$

steps.title: The titration
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)*

A **titration** finds an unknown concentration by measuring exactly what volume of a solution of **known** concentration reacts with it.

**The method.**

1. Use a **pipette** to measure a fixed volume — usually $25.0\text{ cm}^3$ — of the solution of unknown concentration into a **conical flask**.
2. Add a few drops of **indicator**. Methyl orange and phenolphthalein are used because they give a **sharp** colour change; universal indicator does not and is never used.
3. Fill a **burette** with the solution of known concentration and record the starting reading.
4. Add it slowly, swirling, until the indicator changes colour permanently — the **end point**. Record the final reading.
5. The **titre** is the difference between the readings.
6. **Repeat** until you have **concordant** titres, agreeing within $0.10\text{ cm}^3$.

**Only concordant titres are averaged.** The first run is usually rough, and any titre that disagrees is excluded — and you should **say** you excluded it.

For the titres 20.10, 20.05, 20.60, 20.10 cm³, the $20.60$ is discarded and the mean of the remaining three is $20.08\text{ cm}^3$.

**Why the apparatus matters.** A pipette delivers one fixed volume very accurately; a burette measures a variable volume to $0.05\text{ cm}^3$. Using a measuring cylinder for either would make the result far less certain.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Convert to dm³ before anything else.** Write the volume in dm³ on the page as the first line of working. An answer a thousand times too large or too small has almost always skipped this.

**Check the equation before assuming 1 : 1.** For $\mathrm{H_2SO_4} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_2SO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$, the alkali moles are **twice** the acid moles. Questions set this deliberately, and the $1:1$ habit walks straight into it.

**Start from the solution you know completely.** Concentration **and** volume known means you can find its moles; everything else follows from the ratio.

**Average only concordant titres, and say so.** "Excluding the rough titration and the $20.60$ result, the mean of the remaining titres is $20.08\text{ cm}^3$" earns the mark that a bare number does not.

**Justify the apparatus by its uncertainty.** A burette reads to $0.05\text{ cm}^3$ and a pipette delivers one volume very accurately; a measuring cylinder is far coarser, so using one would make the titre — and the final concentration — much less certain.

**Explain why the indicator matters.** Methyl orange and phenolphthalein give a **sharp, single** colour change at the end point. Universal indicator passes through a range of colours, so the end point cannot be judged precisely.

**Watch which solution is in the burette.** The calculation works either way, but the concentration you end up with belongs to whichever solution was the unknown — read the question again before writing the final line.

**Quote a sensible number of significant figures.** Titration data is usually to three, so an answer to six is not more accurate, merely less honest.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- $1\text{ dm}^3 = 1000\text{ cm}^3$ — **convert first, always**.
- $\text{concentration (g/dm}^3) = \dfrac{\text{mass (g)}}{\text{volume (dm}^3)}$.
- *(HT)* $\text{concentration (mol/dm}^3) = \dfrac{\text{moles}}{\text{volume (dm}^3)}$, so $n = c \times V$.
- $\text{g/dm}^3 = \text{mol/dm}^3 \times M_r$; divide to reverse.
- **Titration**: pipette a fixed volume of the unknown, add indicator, run in the known solution from a **burette** to the **end point**.
- Indicators: **methyl orange** or **phenolphthalein**, because the colour change is **sharp**; never universal indicator.
- **Concordant** titres agree within **0.10 cm³**; average only those, and say which you excluded.
- Calculation: moles of the known → **equation ratio** → moles of the unknown → divide by its volume in dm³.
- The ratio is **only** $1:1$ if the equation says so.
- A burette reads to $0.05\text{ cm}^3$; a pipette delivers one fixed volume accurately.
- Quote an answer to about **three significant figures**, matching the data.

questions.prompt: How many cm³ are there in one dm³?
questions.solution: A dm³ is a litre: **1000 cm³**.

questions.prompt: What is the concentration, in g/dm³, of 20 g of solute in 500 cm³ of solution?
Which piece of apparatus measures the variable volume added during a titration?
questions.solution: The **burette** delivers a variable volume and is read to $0.05\text{ cm}^3$. The pipette measures the fixed volume placed in the flask.

questions.prompt: How many moles are there in 25.0 cm³ of a 0.200 mol/dm³ solution?
Why is universal indicator not used in a titration?
options: It changes through a range of colours, so the end point is not sharp
It reacts with the acid that is being added from the burette
It is only accurate when used in strongly alkaline solutions
It cannot be seen clearly against a white tile in the flask
questions.solution: A titration needs a **sharp, single** colour change to judge the end point. Universal indicator passes gradually through several colours, so the exact end point cannot be seen.

questions.prompt: A solution is 0.05 mol/dm³ of sodium hydroxide. What is this in g/dm³? (Mr of NaOH = 40)
Four titres are 18.40, 18.90, 18.45 and 18.35 cm³. Which value should be excluded from the mean?
questions.solution: **18.90 cm³.** The other three span only $0.10\text{ cm}^3$ and are concordant; $18.90$ is well outside that range.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of the concordant titres 18.40, 18.45 and 18.35 cm³? Give your answer to two decimal places.
4 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution. What is its concentration in mol/dm³? (Mr of NaOH = 40)
25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. What is the concentration of the alkali, in mol/dm³?
questions.solution: Moles of acid $= 0.100 \times 0.0200 = 0.00200$. Ratio $1:1$, so alkali is $0.00200\text{ mol}$. Concentration $= \dfrac{0.00200}{0.0250} = $ **0.0800 mol/dm³**.

questions.prompt: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 15.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What is the concentration of the alkali, in mol/dm³?
questions.solution: Moles of acid $= 0.100 \times 0.0150 = 0.00150$. The ratio is $1 : 2$, so the alkali is $2 \times 0.00150 = 0.00300\text{ mol}$. Concentration $= \dfrac{0.00300}{0.0250} = $ **0.120 mol/dm³**. Assuming $1:1$ would halve the answer.

questions.prompt: A student divides the moles of solute by a volume in cm³ instead of dm³. What happens to the answer?
options: It is unchanged, because the units cancel
questions.solution: The volume in cm³ is **1000 times larger** than the same volume in dm³, and dividing by a larger number gives a smaller result — so the concentration comes out **1000 times too small**.

questions.prompt: Explain why a burette rather than a measuring cylinder is used to add the solution of known concentration.
questions.solution: A burette can be read to **0.05 cm³**, far finer than a measuring cylinder, so the **uncertainty in the titre is much smaller**. Since the titre feeds directly into the calculation, a coarser measurement would make the final concentration much less certain.

questions.prompt: A titration gives a mean titre of 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ acid against 25.0 cm³ of alkali in a 1:1 reaction. What is the alkali concentration in g/dm³? (Mr of the alkali = 40)
questions.solution: Moles of acid $= 0.150 \times 0.0200 = 0.00300$. Ratio $1:1$, so alkali $= 0.00300\text{ mol}$. Concentration $= \dfrac{0.00300}{0.0250} = 0.120\text{ mol/dm}^3$. In g/dm³: $0.120 \times 40 = $ **4.8 g/dm³**.

questions.prompt: Why is the first titration in a set usually discarded?
options: It is a rough run used to find the approximate end point
The burette has not been filled accurately at that stage
The indicator needs one run to become effective
The acid is always too concentrated on the first run
questions.solution: The first titration is deliberately **rough**: it locates the end point approximately so that later runs can be added dropwise near it. It is therefore less precise and is excluded from the mean.

questions.prompt: What volume, in cm³, of 0.200 mol/dm³ acid is needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ alkali in a 1:1 reaction?
questions.solution: Moles of alkali $= 0.100 \times 0.0250 = 0.00250$. Ratio $1:1$, so the acid is $0.00250\text{ mol}$. Volume $= \dfrac{n}{c} = \dfrac{0.00250}{0.200} = 0.0125\text{ dm}^3 = $ **12.5 cm³**.

questions.prompt:
A student is asked to find the concentration of a sodium hydroxide solution using 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O.

Describe how they should carry out the titration, and explain how they would use their results to calculate the concentration. Include how they decide which results to use. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
Use a **pipette** to transfer exactly $25.0\text{ cm}^3$ of the sodium hydroxide into a **conical flask**, and add a few drops of **methyl orange** or **phenolphthalein**. Universal indicator must not be used, because it changes through a range of colours and gives no sharp end point.

Fill a **burette** with the $0.100\text{ mol/dm}^3$ hydrochloric acid and record the initial reading. Add the acid to the flask, swirling constantly, until the indicator changes colour **permanently**; near the end point add it dropwise. Record the final reading, and the **titre** is the difference.

**Repeat** until at least two or three titres are **concordant** — agreeing within $0.10\text{ cm}^3$. The first run is rough and is discarded, as is any result outside that range, and the mean is taken of the concordant titres only.

To calculate: moles of acid $= c \times V$, with the mean titre converted to dm³. The equation shows a $1 : 1$ ratio, so the moles of sodium hydroxide are the same. The concentration is then those moles divided by the pipetted volume in dm³ — for a mean titre of $20.0\text{ cm}^3$, that is $\dfrac{0.100 \times 0.0200}{0.0250} = 0.0800\text{ mol/dm}^3$.

examTechnique.body:
Convert every volume to **dm³** before anything else — divide cm³ by 1000. Then it is $n = c \times V$ used twice: forwards on the solution whose concentration and volume you know, and backwards on the unknown.

Between the two, take the ratio from the **balanced equation** — it is only $1:1$ if the equation says so. Average only **concordant** titres, state which you excluded, and quote the answer to about three significant figures.
examinerErrors: Dividing by a volume in cm3.
Assuming a 1 : 1 ratio without reading the equation.
Averaging all the titres, including the rough one.
Not saying which titres were excluded.
Giving the concentration of the wrong solution.
Quoting far more significant figures than the data supports.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes the volumes in dm³ as its first line, takes the mole ratio from the balanced equation rather than assuming it, and works from the solution it knows completely towards the one it does not. It averages only concordant titres and names the ones it excluded and why, justifies the pipette and burette by the uncertainty each gives, explains the indicator choice by the sharpness of the end point, and converts between mol/dm³ and g/dm³ confidently — finishing at a sensible number of significant figures.
